utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IT-94-1-A-R77, allegations against former counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The appearances are as before? Mr. Clegg, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I filed a motion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We must get the record straight. Are you joining the ranks of counsel at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes. I represent the interested party in the contempt proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. So you would like the record to reflect that fact, that you are part of the legal team representing the interested party Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Sorry to pause. I ought to know who I represent, but I certainly do represent the interested party Mr. Tadic. As the Court is well aware, of course, I've been representing him in the appeal, and I certainly, for today, wish to make a motion to this Chamber on his behalf. So in that limited extent, I represent him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The bench approves of your addressing the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And you're speaking of a motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I am. It's a motion that was filed on the 26th of August of this year, and I would ask for the Chamber to go into closed session for me to address the matters raised therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Any objections from any party, interested party?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar, would you take the necessary steps?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I noticed Mr. Vujin and Mr. Domazet don't appear to be in the chamber. I don't know where they've gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I am grateful to you for pointing out that. I had assumed that all parties were in court at this time. Perhaps we might await word from the Registrar, who might have an explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: You had been very clear. You said that we were going to resume after 30 minutes of break, at 12.00, so the parties are supposed to be ready to participate in the hearing at the due time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We have at last Mr. Vujin and Mr. Domazet, and we are in a position -- we have with us Mr. Vujin and Mr. Domazet, and we are now in a position to resume the proceedings proper. The next witness, I believe, is Mr. Brkic. Is that right, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Quite, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic has been sent for, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The request has been made. He should be here in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Brkic, I believe, is your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, would you give the date of birth of your good self, as well as the place of birth?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I was born on 11th November, 1956 in Ljubovia (phoen) in the Republic of Serbia in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And now would you please state your occupation?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I'm a journalist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And where do you now live?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade, the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, you made certain statements. Have you seen them recently?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can the statements be made available to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If you wish me to, I could number the three statements from now on so that they can be more easily referenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement made in a newspaper, together with a photograph, will be number 8, Exhibit 8. Then there is a statement made on the 8th of February, 1999. This will be Exhibit 9. Finally, a statement, the latest date for which is the 18th of February, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That would be 10?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, I forgot that, Your Honour. This will be Exhibit 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, do have a look at those statements.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is true that as a journalist I'm the author of the text that has been shown me. It is true that I myself have signed the statement. It is true that under full moral and legal responsibility I gave the statement that you have shown me and I stand behind it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You affirm today the accuracy of the contents of those statements?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Have the statements been made available to the interested parties? Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, we haven't. I haven't this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say I'm very surprised to say that. The statements were admitted into evidence on the -- forgive me -- I believe on the 24th of February of this year. That is the scheduling order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, did you see a scheduling order of the 24th of February of this year, attaching copies of those statements? Mr. Registrar, may I suggest you show Mr. Domazet the scheduling order with copies of the attached statements.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Then may we proceed on the basis that those statements are formally admitted into evidence. Now, Mr. Brkic, I would like you to turn to Exhibit number 9. That is to say, your statement of 8 February 1999. Would I be correct in summarising your statements to mean this: That you are asserting that Mr. Vujin had been manipulating evidence and undermining the presentation of the case for Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And that he was part of a machinery of the state for ensuring that persons connected with the state were not exposed to any risks through the defence of anyone in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not with the state but with the state leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: State leadership. And I understand you also to be saying that that was also the policy regardless of whether or not the effective defence of an accused person necessitated reference to allegations against officials connected with the state.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I shall try to answer you in two words. The state police ordered the State Security Service that by a certain group of advocates, amongst them Mr. Vujin, to exert control over the detained individuals which this Tribunal have been charged with war crimes. The intention of the state leadership was to exert control over those individuals so that their Defence counsel do not expand responsibility to include higher command structures, police structures, and the state leadership. The text that I published, which has been attached here, already in 1995, I presented this plan of the state leadership. Unfortunately, the events completely confirm the quotations made in my text, and one individual was made to commit suicide to -- in order not to testify against others. I don't know whether I can have three more words, whether the rules allow me to explain this procedure and how this was planned, how it was planned that the Defence counsel at the Tribunal should exert influence on the accused to instruct them how to behave towards the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brkic, I appreciate those observations, which lead me to the penultimate paragraph of your statement of 8 February, 1999. In that statement you say: "I'm aware of the consequences of bearing false testimony, and I am prepared to confirm before the International Criminal Tribunal the truthfulness of the assertions in the above-mentioned text." And likewise in your statement of the 18th February, 1999, in paragraph numbered 5, at the end you stated this: "I do not merely believe that Mr. Vujin undermined Mr. Dusan Tadic's defence. I have concrete proof of this which I cannot present in this written answer." Now, as you will appreciate, the Appeals Chamber would be interested in knowing what is the concrete proof that you could provide.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I made this statement on the 8th and 18th of February, the state in which I live and where I come from at the time, after it was thought that it would be at war. The circumstances have completely changed since then, and those of us who live in Serbia, we say "good morning" and we count each other to see whether we are all there. If I were to present to you the names of the people from this State Security Service who gave me a plan of activity, and proof, documents of the activities of the lawyers before the International Tribunal, please believe me, I would write the death sentence for those people. I would have signed their death sentence. So I cannot take this upon myself, this responsibility and this courage. I have no personal reasons for accusing either Mr. Vujin or any other lawyers. I do this exclusively by virtue of my conscience and to thwart their activities; that is to say, to sell out their clients and bring them in a situation in which they are not able to defend themselves. I too was accused many times as a journalist, and I know what it means to come before a court and to have to prove yourself. If I were to tell you the names of those people, and as the hearings are public, then please believe me that their lives would be worthless. You will make the decision yourselves about whether I was truthful or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So I understand you to be taking this position: That to make good the concrete proof which you stated you could present, you would have to call the names of individuals and that that would expose them to unnecessary risks.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Not unnecessary risk, but their lives would be in danger. Your Honours, by an order of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Slobodan Milosevic at the time, a state commission was set up which was to have studied the responsibilities of the head of the state security in giving facts to me, because I have had many documents, and Slobodan Milosevic published these. I have published many of them, but there was no way in which this could be linked to the responsibility of the head of the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me take you to the article which you wrote, Exhibit 8, at page 5, top paragraph, in English. I don't know what it is in the version before you, but it's the paragraph in which you stated that: "Attorney Toma Fila has forever ruined the career and life of actor Zarko Lausevic." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I remember, yes, as I am the author of the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, in that paragraph you are referring to a meeting at which you say Mr. Vujin was present, and you say that at that meeting Mr. Fila said, "Gentlemen, there is no client whom I cannot sell. I am the biggest Judas of all and am proud of it." What is the basis upon which you make that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I published the text which you have just read out to me in part, I was invited to the State Security Service. I cannot tell you the name of the individual who showed me a programme of activity of that service, and that it followed orders from the President of the Republic of the Yugoslavia, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic. That task and assignment was to select a group of attorneys to come before to the Tribunal, your Tribunal, to defend the accused accused of war crimes. And that group of lawyers was carefully selected on the basis of the dossiers that they had on them in the State Security Service. The lawyers were given the task of controlling the accused, of contacting the accused, of threatening them that they should not in their testimony implicate others, to tell them that their families were in Yugoslavia in a difficult situation, that they would be persecuted and, if necessary, to compel them to submit suicide. That was the plan which, for me, was a monstrous plan at the time, and I couldn't believe it, in fact, but as this was told to me by a man working in the State Security Service and who occupied such a high position, I had to believe him. I wrote this article as a result, and, unfortunately, life has proved that this was so, and I wrote the text in 1995. I would like to have been wrong, that this was just one more bad newspaper article. When one finds oneself in a prison in another country, he is alone. He has the prosecutors, he has the judges, and his natural ally is his lawyer. It is the lawyer through which he has contact with the outside, and it is the lawyer who helps him to function socially, Your Honours. The role of lawyers in communism and the country that I come from was that this last straw, whether we're talking about a serious criminal or not, it was the task to cut that straw. Some Serbian lawyers used their profession and handed their clients on a plate, and they remained completely helpless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, can you tell me this: Did the material which you had enable you to say what was the reaction of Mr. Vujin when Mr. Fila said, "Gentlemen, there is no client whom I cannot sell. I'm the biggest Judas of all, and I'm proud of it"?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: The member of the State Security Service or the functionary which gave me these facts recounted to me the contents of the talk with the group of lawyers who were called to the security service. I do not know in precise terms whether they were individual talks or whether they were all invited collectively, to a collective meeting, so that I cannot tell you in precise terms, but I did make a note of those words taken from my conversation with the man working for the State Security Service who invited me to present the plan of his service vis-a-vis the lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did that information enable you to tell whether Mr. Vujin was present when Mr. Fila made that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as the journalist who had come to get certain information, as I say, I wasn't too curious, I wasn't too inquisitive, because my position was one of a journalist, and it did not allow me to be too inquisitive and curious. I just listened to what was being told to me, and you will probably admit that had I gone into details, I would have lost the confidence of the man who had invited me there. He gave me as much information as he saw fit, as he thought necessary, if you understand me, and this is the natural relationship between the person giving out information and the person receiving information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Should I then take it that the limitations within which you work did not enable you to tell whether Mr. Vujin was present when Mr. Fila made that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I personally was convinced that he was present and that a dialogue of this kind had taken place. Your Honours, if I may, I have just recalled one point. Before I published the article, the editor in chief of the paper in which the text appeared asked me for proof. He wanted to see whether he would be able to prove the truthfulness of the allegations in the text because otherwise we would have probably been sued for high amounts, and I myself would have had to have rigid responsibilities. I asked to be received by the individual at the State Security Service, and he gave me a piece of paper to sign for keeping secrets and confidentiality. He did give me some notes. I showed this to my editor in chief. We sealed the envelope, we returned the printed matter, and the article went forward. If it means anything to you, I published the article in an opposition paper. The State Security Service, by nature of their jobs, are there to protect the state leadership. So I do not believe that the information that I was given was false, was incorrect, because they had no reason to do this, apart from the fact that as individuals, they might not have agreed with what was being done, that it was below their dignity, and this, one day, would ultimately do our country more harm. I think that they did this for those reasons, but I leave it to you to assess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Indeed. In Exhibit 9, in the second paragraph, you do, indeed, say: "I published this text after the editorial board's decision that I should give the editor in chief proof of the truthfulness of the text and the assertions contained therein," and in your testimony, you alluded to the risk of your being sued. Has there been any litigation between you and Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the six lawyers who were mentioned on this list have filed a charge with the court for the harm done. This was done in 1995. They had in mind procedural matters, and I think that it would have taken effect up to now. I was a witness in a court of law, although a ruling has not yet been made. I know that two lawyers of the six have withdrawn charges, of the six that tendered charges. I can give you their names. They are Branimir Gugl and Nebojsa Pavlovic, and they said that they do not feel that they have been libelled. Mr. Fila filed the charge for remuneration of damages, and they said that their signatures were used. At the court in Belgrade, several judges took their turn in the case, and as I followed the work of the court in my professional work and I know most of the judges in Belgrade, one of the judges -- I wanted to show to one of the judges what I had at my disposal, the records and official notes made by the State Security Service, and she said, "Well, we don't need that. We all know who all those attorneys are. You don't have to prove anything to us. We're well aware of that." A ruling has not yet been made. The judgement has not yet been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me take you specifically to your relations with Mr. Vujin. Has there been any litigation between the two of you in respect of any of these allegations which you have made?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin is one of these six lawyers who filed charges against me in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Following our usual procedure, I would now invite Mr. Abell to ask any questions; thereafter, the Prosecution and then Mr. Vujin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, I represent Dusko Tadic in these proceedings, who is an interested party to the contempt proceedings against Mr. Vujin. I would like to start by asking you about the litigation that you were just asked about. You told us that there were six lawyers who sued yourself, and amongst those six lawyers was Mr. Milan Vujin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Was the litigation against you personally or against you and your newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Against the newspaper, against the newspaper because the newspaper carried the story, and I testified as the author of that story.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: So you were a witness, but the defendant in the litigation was the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: The newspaper. Yes, they were the legal person, the publisher; that is to say, the newspaper publishing house Srpska Rec, and I was only called in as a witness, and I testified before the court as a sworn witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: What stage have the proceedings against the newspaper reached?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: To be quite truthful, I can present only my very own point of view. I don't think that the courts or the prosecutors are interested in bringing these proceedings to an end. Otherwise, if we take into account how much time has elapsed, this should have been over three years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: The action, the litigation, commenced when?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: If you wish to have a precise answer, the trial started in 1995. Marina Govedarica was the presiding judge, and that chamber rejected the charges that were brought against the paper. They said that due process was not taken into account. Toma Fila, they say, did not know how to actually compose this report. He brought charges against a newspaper, and the newspaper is not a legal person, according to the law that is valid in Yugoslavia, and that is why the court had to reject this paper --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Pause, please. The question I asked was when the litigation started, and the answer is, to your knowledge, in 1995. To your knowledge, has there ever been a judgement in the proceedings against your newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first judgement was passed in 1996. It happened in Belgrade; that is to say, this document was rejected as impermissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: In other words, it was a judgement in favour of the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The district court that ruled on this, and I was involved, I had the status of an involved person, I said that obviously the accused have a poor lawyer, Mr. Toma Fila, who is not very knowledgable in matters of law, and it would be a good thing to take this back and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, I'm going to interrupt you and stop you. I wanted you to clarify that the judgement that you speak of was not against the newspaper; it was against the people who had brought the proceedings, had brought the litigation. Am I right in that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you're quite right, and I thought that I was quite accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: What I want to ask you now is, to your knowledge, has there, in proceedings brought by Mr. Vujin and others against your newspaper, ever been a judgement against you in this matter?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Sir, they could have started action on several scores -- that is to say, libel, criminal proceedings -- and then they could also seek compensation, so there could have been several courses of action taken. I already said that the initial judgement rejected all of this for formal reasons because they had not composed their criminal report, because they brought charges against perpetrators unknown, and the newspaper itself is not a legal person, as I already said. I already said to you that the judgement was in favour of Srpska Rec, the publisher the charges were brought against, and it was against the persons who brought charges because their legal counsel, Mr. Toma Fila, did not know how to compose the document containing charges according to the law on litigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, given what you've said to us, to look, please, at a document which is at pages 602, really, to 617, which is in a filing made on the 23rd of April of this year by Mr. Vujin, information submitted by Mr. Vujin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: As I say, it should be in Your Honours' papers at page 602 through to 617, 618. A scheduling order, on my pagination, is at page 634, if that assists. Could it please be shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I appreciate, Mr. Brkic, that that document you've been given is in English. It was filed, to the best of my knowledge, by Mr. Vujin in English, and I don't believe -- at least if there is, I've never seen it -- that there is any Serbo-Croat, Yugoslavian original document of which that is a translation. But I want you, please, to look, if you can, at page 611, top right, 6-1-1, top right.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I imagine that these were the charges brought against -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I don't know whether Your Honours have copies or whether it would be easier if the document is put on the epidiascope so that the Court can follow the document at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That will certainly be helpful to me because I am not in the happy position of having the documents, and I believe there are other colleagues who are in the similar position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just intervene at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In the brief that I sent by mail, in addition to all the texts that were translated into English that I sent by fax in order to save time, I sent to the Court the originals or rather photocopies of these documents in the Serbo-Croat language, and I'm sure that the Court should have these documents in the Serbian language as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujin. Mr. Abell, are you in a position to proceed? Is the witness handicapped in any way?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, we shall have to see. The document is in English. For reasons which will become apparent in a moment, if I can just say, for reasons which will become apparent in a moment, the originals may be very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin is signalling that he has an original.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: That's helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document could be numbered as being Exhibit 11 because we do not have the original in Serbo-Croatian in our files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Any objections from the Prosecution? No objections. Then the document is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: May I see the document before it's passed to the witness, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be free to leave for five minutes, please? I have to go to my car only for five minutes in order to get the originals of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have understood the substance of these documents, and I do not need the originals in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, you've heard what the witness has said. It's now ten minutes to one. We will be breaking off shortly, and you may then conveniently go to your car for any additional material you may require. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: What I want to ask you, Mr. Brkic, is this: The document which we have in English -- I wonder if it could be put on the screen so people can follow it. On page 611, the first page of the document, it appears to be -- 611. Could it be moved, please, so we could see the top of the document? Further down. Thank you. It appears to be a translation of a document, and it says: "Law office, Fila, First Municipal Court in Belgrade, Belgrade," filed on April the 27th, 1995, and then there are a list of Prosecutors, Tomo Fila; Guberina; Milan Vujin from New Belgrade, with an address; and then there are various other names. Are those the lawyers to which you have just referred to, Mr. Brkic, who are suing your newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, these are the lawyers concerned. With your permission, I have here before me the original, rather, a copy of the original that the court or, rather, Judge Govedarica ruled on this and actually rejected this, and I already said her name was Govedarica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I know. Can I come to that in a moment? The accused, still on that page, is Slobodne Novine, Srpska Rec. Is that a Serb word? That's for "newspaper"?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: "Srpska Rec" is the newspaper, and "Slobodne," that is a qualification. A newspaper is a newspaper, and whether a newspaper is opposition or pro-government, or free or not free, that is a question of taste, and that is why a newspaper cannot be called a free newspaper, Slobodne. They didn't even know how to compose this document. As I said, they could have brought charges against Srpska Rec. Srpska Rec is a legal person. They have a giro account, et cetera, et cetera. But why did they put this, "Slobodne"? I mean, that shows you how professional these lawyers are, begging your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, that's the name of the newspaper then. Then we see that the suit, the litigation, is for compensation for damage in issue 199 of the magazine for March the 13th of 1995, and the headline, if the clerk can kindly move it up, the headline is the journalist, Milovan Brkic, titled "Secret Police Travels to The Hague", with the subheadline "The Lawyers Provocateurs First Extort the Confession From Their Clients and Then Deliver Them to the Police." Is that a reference to the article that you have referred to in your two statements which were filed before this Court?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I want to, before the luncheon adjournment, move to the point that I'm trying to make. If we go now, please, to page 608, although the page number is before 611, this, in fact, is page 4 of that document, because the court pagination, forgive me, appears to be in reverse. On that page, towards the bottom, do we see "The Judgement: The accused Slobodne Novine 'Srpska Rec' from Belgrade is obliged to pay the prosecutors as the compensation for the non-material damage of psyche injury," it reads, "to Toma Fila for the injury of his honour and reputation and the honour and reputation of his father late Filota File the amount of 10,000.00 dinars, to Veljko Guberina for the injury of his honour and reputation the amount of 10,000.00 dinars, to Milan Vujin for the injury of his honour and his reputation the amount of 10,000.00 dinars," and so it goes on, in other words, purporting to be a judgement against the newspaper? Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I understand, but I think that you have not understood. This is the proposal of a judgement that is mentioned in the charges that are brought against a person. You have to -- when you're filing charges against someone, you have to say what kind of a ruling you would like the court to pass and this is just a proposal. Have you understood what I said?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Is it in any way a final judgement against the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I think we have not understood each other at all. You quoted a document to me which are the charges that were brought by the lawyers. When they bring charges before a court of law, then they have to propose a judgement, what they would like the judgement to be. So you can see this in the Serbian original. Then it is the court that passes the judgement. I'm sorry. You are not familiar with our criminal procedure and legislation, but according to our criminal legislation, when a party brings charges before a court of law, then they have to put in this document what kind of a judgement they would like the court to pass. It would be very regrettable if we did not understand one another because these are very important things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I agree, and I want to be clear, and if I'm the only one who is not, the position is this: That this is not a final judgement. You're saying it's merely a lawyer's document inviting the court to make that judgement in the future; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I have more questions to put after lunch. I'm going to move from that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abell. This is a convenient -- yes, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the Prosecution could beg the indulgence of the Appeals Chamber and ask to go into private session for a clarification before the luncheon recess, not closed but private, as to a matter earlier decided, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You assure the bench it will not necessitate any considerable extension of time beyond --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- 1.00? Mr. Registrar, you can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.07 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The sitting is resumed. Mr. Yapa, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I have an application to make, Your Honour. May I be excused from the rest of the proceedings this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Indeed. Mr. Abell, you were on your legs at the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I was, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Do be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, I want to continue to ask you questions, and I don't want you for one moment to misunderstand me in the questions I was asking you before lunch. I am not suggesting that there was a judgement by the court against your newspaper. I simply wanted your evidence to confirm that the case was not decided in favour of Mr. Vujin. In case anybody who saw the papers that I showed you before lunch had misunderstood and thought that that was actually a judgement, I wanted your evidence to say there was none. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I've understood now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us leave that topic alone now. I have a series of questions for you, and it will help me and it may help Their Honours, if you, as I'm sure you will, listen carefully to my questions and try to answer just the question I ask. If I want more information from you, I'll ask it. All right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Firstly, can I ask you this: Do you know Dusko Tadic personally?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Do you know any member of his family personally?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Vujin personally?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Have you met him?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Have you ever been present at any meetings or conversations that he has had?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I was present with one of my colleagues, the editor of Student, in the office of Mr. Guberina in which Mr. Vujin was also present and a lady, Mrs. Mara Pilipovic, who works in the same office as Mr. Vujin. I think that we were even on friendly terms. That is what we could term them. That is how I envisaged them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Do you have any personal grudge or bias against Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: No, I personally do not. Really, I do not. I have never had any personal conflicts with Mr. Vujin. For your information, Mr. Fila's offices have sued me on several occasions with regard to their clients, but we are on very good terms. We sit down together, we talk together, and it's their job to do what is their job, and luckily, they have brought no charges, nothing personal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Do you have any particular favouritism or feelings towards Mr. Tadic or bias towards him?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I see the man for the first time. I can only suppose that the man sitting over there is Mr. Dusko Tadic, but I have never seen him before. I just know that our police turned him over in Germany, that is, they took him to Germany for him to be turned over to the Tribunal, for them to bring an indictment against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: My question was: Do you have any personal favouritism or bias towards Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot have any personal favouritism for somebody who I did not know existed. I don't know where he comes from, I know none of Mr. Tadic's family, and I am not really interested, that is to say, I have no relationship towards the acts that he performed. Whether he's guilty or not, that is something for the Tribunal to ascertain. So I cannot comment and, therefore, I have no personal relationship towards him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you. What is it that drove you or motivated you to make the two statements that you -- well, no, firstly, the article which you wrote, the newspaper article which is attached to the two statements that have been filed in this Court? What is it that drove you or motivated you to write that article?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I wanted, as a journalist, to inform the public of the Republic of Serbia, the state in which I live, that our political leadership is endeavouring to behave in such a way as to obstruct the International Tribunal in a way that is not -- does not befit it, and I wanted to inform my readers of the intentions of the regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Were you aware, when you wrote the article, that it obviously contains serious allegations about members of the legal profession?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: At all events, I consider myself to be a responsible individual and against me as a journalist, and I have always given my all to the profession. I have given my life to the profession in the struggle for democracy in my own country, and I risked my own life in doing so. More than 570 times criminal charges were brought against me for slander, liable and so forth by the protagonists of the state. Of the 570 charges brought against me, I have only lost one case with the son of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic. The court concluded in that particular case that I presented untruths with regard to the property and riches of the son of the president of Yugoslavia, Mr. Milosevic, and I had to pay compensation, fines. But from all the others you can deduce whether I have done my job professionally or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: So out of 570 cases brought against you, 569 you have won is what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you help me about this -- forgive me, but back to the question I asked you which is this: When you wrote the article, presumably you realised that it contained serious allegations against members of the legal profession in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: As you're asking me that question, I suppose that you know of the country I live in, and that for assertions and allegations of that kind in a text you can be brought before a criminal court of law. You can lose a lot of money and you can lose your head, because privately any associate of the regime or criminal can ask for your head and ask for your murder. I had no personal reason to subject myself to that danger. I wanted to help the democratic forces in the country so that in my own country too conditions could be made for democratic institutions to flourish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, may I ask you to explore a little more this aspect, whether these slander actions were of a criminal nature or a civil nature?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Can I just deal with this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, you have really answered the next question that I was going to ask, which was that you are aware of the consequences of telling such serious lies if they are lies?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I may, I would like to quote the example of 1987, when I published an article in a newspaper which was published in Ljubljana, Slovenia, a text and the title of "There Are People at Play in Our Country of Serbia", and I set out the initial policies of the president, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic. I analysed his personal and family circumstances. As I say, I analysed his personal and family circumstances, and because of that text which was published in Slovenia, that is to say, in another republic, the magistrate in Belgrade gave me 50 days imprisonment for violating the repute of social and political organisations, and nothing like that existed in any laws of the world apart from that of Hitler's Germany and in Stalin's code of law. So I spent 15 days in prison, but the Supreme Court of the Republic of Serbia refuted its sentence and set me free. That is to say, fined me with a fine of 1.000 dinars because I did not give my correct address. For that incrimination I paid the fee and the fine and I was released. So I am conscious of the repercussions of the articles I write and the risks I run in writing those texts, of course, if the facts are incorrect and unsubstantiated. I am not a masochist, nor am I a psychopath to go against me, so it is very difficult to prove the correctness of your quotations, particularly if -- even if you do do so in a court of law. This has no repercussions on the people that you have quoted, and 20 per cent of my texts, luckily, that I have published were initiated by proceedings against people who abuse their functions, state functions, political functions, or functions within courts of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Please pause there, Mr. Brkic. Just help me with this question, just to clarify the situation. If this article that you had written was a tissue of lies in the allegations it makes against Mr. Vujin and his colleagues, would you be subject just to possible civil liable action or could you be subject to a criminal charge in your country?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Vujin, the lawyer, could, according to the Criminal Code, bring in a criminal charge against me on the basis of Article 92 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Serbia, that is the criminal action of slander and liable, and Article 93 of the Republic of Serbia. For that kind of crime you can go to prison for one year. The prison sentence is a maximum of one year, or if the prosecutor has proved that there were more serious violations, then the imprisonment can be from six months to three years imprisonment. The criminal charge -- Mr. Milan Vujin or the other lawyers did not file criminal charges against me, nor did they mention me as the individual encompassed in the charge and action, although, according to the law on public information in the Republic of Serbia, which was in force at the time, according to Article 13, I was subject for a misdemeanour, but as I say, they only sued the paper and not myself as the author of the article. By filing a criminal charge, this does not exclude proceedings and litigation. They are two actions that can be brought parallelly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: So in other words, you could personally have been sued in the civil courts for liable and also been made a defendant in criminal proceedings if this article contains lies about Mr. Vujin and his colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: In the criminal proceedings I could only have been responsible, because I was the author of the text. So I could only have been incorporated in this criminal proceeding. In the civil courts, according to Article 13 of the Law on Public Information for Serbia, which was abolished last year but was strict at the time in the extreme sense for payment of fines, and it is the publisher of the newspaper that could have been -- that charges could have been filed against. So I was left out of all that. I was left out of the action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your editor, he obviously would have seen your article before a decision was made to publish it in the newspaper; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Is he also a man who is well aware of the consequences of publishing serious lies that could damage an important man's reputation, in his newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you consider us coming from Serbia citizens of the Third Order, but the man editing the paper is a serious man and, therefore, I see no reason for you to ask me questions which -- do you want to say that we are all irresponsible?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: No. You may misunderstand me. I'm not trying to suggest that at all. I'm trying to establish that you as a journalist, and your editor as a newspaper editor, would not be in the business of publishing serious lies. That's what I'm trying to establish from you, bring out in your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: In the society in which I live and in the state in which I live, sir, the publication of falsehoods is not only sanctioned legally but my very life can be in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Does it come to this: That you were driven to publish that article because it was the truth from your investigations, and because you considered that it was a serious enough situation that your investigations had uncovered that it should be published and made known to the public?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I deeply believe in freedom and democracy. My people, unfortunately, are not free, and in the state that I come from there is no democracy. This is shown by the fact that the key people in my country have been indicted by this Tribunal for the gravest of crimes. Being a journalist and publishing articles, including the one that we are discussing right now, I wanted to avoid new scandals. I believed that one day the role of our lawyers in the defence of indictees before The Hague Tribunal would finally be revealed. At that time I could not have envisaged that proceedings would be initiated against Mr. Vujin before this Tribunal. I did not initiate these proceedings. I published this article four years ago. I believe that you do not think that I am a prophet and that I was in a position to foresee this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: The question was: Were you driven to write and have published this article because your investigation showed that it was the truth? It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: If it were not the truth, I would not have published the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just want to ask you one or two questions to expand one or two points that you raise in the article. Could we please look at page 2 of the article?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: If it assists Your Honours, it probably doesn't, but the top right it's page 5356. Page 2, bottom right of the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Do you have it, Mr. Brkic? You have the original in your language. If it helps, I will read out the paragraph that I am referring to: "When the possibility of trying war criminals was announced and the proposal for establishing a International Tribunal was put forward, the president," there's a gap which isn't legible, "the president of the Serbian bar association, Milan Vujin, and statements by Mr. Guberina, they all denigrated the idea of trying war criminals." Do you have that passage?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you are asking me whether it is true that all lawyers who appear before the International Criminal Tribunal as defence counsel for the accused, in their statements, and in the bar association of Serbia, and in the Yugoslav and Serb media reject --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, counsel is only asking you at this time if you have located the passage in the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, please don't worry. I'm just trying to do -- I'm just trying to make sure that you --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Translation is no good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: All right. Please listen, Mr. Brkic. I'm trying to make sure that you have got the paragraph that I am trying to ask you about. That's all. I'm not making any accusations. I'm not attacking you, Mr. Brkic, at all. I hope you understand me. I just want you to identify the paragraph. Okay? If it helps, I have it in the English translation, two or three paragraphs down from a heading "Opposed But Ready". I don't know if that helps you, Mr. Brkic. And the paragraph describes a declaration --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: -- denigrating the trying of war criminals. Tell me when you've found that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, this translation is no good or, rather, the photocopy is no good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Do you mean the original newspaper article?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You can see it from there, can't you? See? It's a very bad photocopy. I know what I wrote in the text but I can't find it here. See? You can see what a poor photocopy it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I don't know whether there exists with the Tribunal a better photocopy. The only document that has reached me is the English translation. I think I'm the same as everyone else, all the other lawyers in the case, all the other parties.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I found it. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Good. Thank you, Mr. Brkic.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: It says all of them were opposed to the idea of trying individuals for war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Does that include Mr. Milan Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mr. Vujin often appeared in the media, and he denied the right of The Hague Tribunal to try war criminals, and then he said that this court was unfounded, and that they were not in charge, and that the United Nations were not entitled to set up ad hoc Tribunals for war crimes and that the aim of this was to discredit Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Were you ever present at any meeting, either private or public, to hear Mr. Vujin expressing those views?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I watched Mr. Vujin on television. I saw him appear on TV programmes and I read what he said in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And it was on that topic, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, on that topic, on the topic of the attitude of the Yugoslav judiciary towards the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: So opposed to the Tribunal, opposed to the work of the Tribunal, and opposed to discrediting Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: They believed that the Tribunal was a political means of pressure against the Serbs and that it was created with a view to depicting Serbs as criminals in the eyes of the world. It did not recognise the legitimacy and legality of the Tribunal, but they all came to defend persons accused before this very same Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: So in our English translation, just a few lines further down: "When the Serbian Bar Association received a polite call to draw up a list of ten attorneys and send it to the Tribunal," do you have that part?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I know I wrote that, yes. Yes, I can see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Just read the paragraph to yourself. You say: "The same lawyers who vowed that 'In the name of constitutional principles, we must not allow the surrender of our people' made a secret list in the State Security Service signing a statement that they would loyally cooperate with the service and that as defence counsel, they would report on the behaviour of suspects in court." What was the basis of your saying that, that there was a secret list of lawyers who would cooperate with the service, UDBA, and report on the behaviour of suspects?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I already told you that I had established contact with a man in a high position in the State Security Service, and he showed me this list that was made up and was headed by Mr. Vujin. I think at that time, he was the president of the bar association of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: That is Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Would you have ever published such a thing if you had not been convinced that it was a true fact?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I never would have published it otherwise because, indeed, I hold nothing against Mr. Vujin. Would any normal person accuse anyone of that? What would be my reasons for doing that? Why would I expose myself to the danger of being criminally charged and being tried and being ordered to pay fines, et cetera? After all, various persons could say, "Look, this man is persecuting me. Take care of him." Of course I would not have exposed myself to all of that had I not profoundly believed in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Can we go to a place a little further in your article?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's near the bottom of page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: "Sources acquainted with the work of this group of provocateurs from the ranks of attorneys claim that the preparation and special training of Hague attorneys has already begun to make them capable of controlling their clients, to warn them to keep their mouths shut and to be careful not to get carried away and denigrate Serbian leaders." Again, would you have contemplated publishing such a thing if you had not been convinced that it was the truth?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: No. No, I, indeed, would not have written that otherwise for various reasons, for several reasons. Persons who were already aware that they were going to The Hague, I mean, I would not want to upset them, that they would have to face such lawyers. I would not wish to expose the State of Serbia to yet a new shameful thing that could compromise it even more before the international public.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Was Mr. Vujin, from the information you received, one of these people you referred to as Hague attorneys involved in controlling their clients, warning them to keep their mouths shut and not to get carried away and denigrate Serbian leaders?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Whether he did that in the case of Mr. Tadic or not, I do not know. But I know that as for the plans of the State Security Service, he held a significant position in those plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin held a significant position in those plans, if this is a fair way of putting it, to control --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: The secret service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: -- to control defendants before the Tribunal, to prevent them implicating, saying anything that may implicate other people as yet undetected?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Does that include, if need be, to control their clients for the "good of the state" even at the expense of those individual defendants' own chances of putting forward a proper defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Individuals indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal are of no significance whatsoever to the state leadership of the country. They only wanted them not to go too far in their defence, and they had their families as hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I just want to ask you one or two questions, Mr. Brkic, about the two statements that you made dated the 8th of February of this year and the 18th of February of this year. Please go with me to the one dated the 18th of February. I want now to be very specific about Mr. Tadic's case and Mr. Vujin. You make an assertion or a conclusion in your evidence, in your written statement, number 2: "I have information that he controlled evidence," that is, Mr. Vujin, "in the case of the criminal proceedings against Mr. Dusko Tadic and that he manipulated the evidence on the orders of the Serbian MUP ..." Help us with that. "MUP" is?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Ministry of the Interior. Within the Ministry of the Interior is the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Reading on: "... and the Information and Documentation Service of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs with the aim of preventing Mr. Dusko Tadic from implicating other perpetrators in his testimony before the Tribunal and exposing high officials in Republika Srpska, Serbia, and Montenegro to prosecution. This information comes from the highest ranks of the Serbian MUP." Then at paragraph 5, you say: "I do not merely believe that Mr. Vujin undermined Mr. Dusko Tadic's defence. I have concrete proof of this which I cannot present in this written answer." Those two paragraphs pose a very serious question, Mr. Brkic. Are they the truth as you know it to be from your investigations and your information?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether my statement will make Mr. Tadic's defence more difficult, but I'm going to tell you the truth, and I hope Mr. Tadic will forgive me. The wife of Mr. Tadic is not a citizen of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and Mr. Vujin made it possible for Mrs. Tadic to obtain Yugoslav citizenship. Of course, the granting of citizenship was a protracted process, and when Mr. Dusan Tadic became aware or, rather, when he withdrew his power of attorney, when he did not want Mr. Vujin to represent him anymore, Mr. Vujin helped the family of the accused Tadic financially from the money that he got from the Tribunal for the defence of Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: The question I ask is whether the statements you make in paragraph 2 and 5 of your statement are the truth.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want me to explain how I came to know this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes, I was just about to ask you. Did you have a source? I'm not asking you at the moment to name that person, but did you have a source or sources for this information?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. A man from the State Security Service showed me that Mr. Tadic, when he talked to the investigators in the International Criminal Tribunal, he "talked a lot", and that he told the Tribunal about everything that he knew that was going on in Republika Srpska, and that his defence had implicated quite a few persons in Republika Srpska as persons who had committed grave crimes against humanity, and that is what this Tribunal was set up for. He asked his defence counsel, Mr. Vujin, to investigate this, to go and to see people who could testify on behalf of his defence, and Mr. Vujin, underground, refused to send the statements that he obtained with Mara Pilipovic underground, he refused to send them to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did you speak face to face with this source within the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a very important individual, and I could not but believe him because he had no personal reasons whatsoever to speak otherwise of these questions. Several people would be arrested some day, and this proved to be true, and these people that Mr. Tadic mentioned, indeed, were arrested afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Were you satisfied that your source within the security service was a source independent of Mr. Tadic himself?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I was not satisfied to have heard such things, but I trusted my source. I did not pay him. He was not motivated to sell information to me, as is done, for example, in Western countries, for example, in the United States of America and in other countries where journalists pay people for providing information. He gave me information free of charge, running the risk that I might tell someone who told me all of this, and perhaps this would entail grave consequences for him. So this was a risk that he did run.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did you ever see anything in writing at all when you had a conversation or conversations with this, as you say, high-up source within the security service?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: He had a file, he had papers, but I trusted him. I did not ask him to have a look myself at these papers because, after all, how should I put this, he could have written these statements himself. I don't know how these things are done, but I trusted him. In such affairs, you either have to trust a person or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Had you had conversations on other occasions with this individual, I don't mean about Mr. Tadic, but had you had conversations with this individual on other occasions where he had given you information?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and quite a few articles --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Did that information that he'd given you on other occasions ever prove to be wrong or unreliable?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: No. No, otherwise, I would not have used him, no. No one in the state that I come from could believe how come I came to receive such information. They thought that I was in the employ of foreign intelligence services, that I was working for some foreign agency or for the KGB or whoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Are you able to give any specific example, Mr. Brkic, of how it was that Mr. Vujin undermined the defence of Mr. Tadic before the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, as he was defending himself from the accusations brought against him, asked his defence attorney to go to the places where he had allegedly committed crimes and to talk to other people who could testify on his behalf and who could prove that he had not committed the crimes that he was charged with having committed. Mr. Vujin had also employed Mara Pilipovic from his office, and she talked to persons who could have testified on his behalf in his defence, and they could have refuted this thesis, that he had committed crimes. I think that this was Mr. Simo Drlaca, and it was his operations in that part of Republika Srpska that were supposed to be concealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Who was doing the concealing?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vujin had statements made by various persons and also the notes made by his assistant, Mr. Mara Pilipovic, but he did not inform Mr. Tadic about this and he did not intend to present this in court so that the Court could have insight into the activities of the accused and other persons who at that time were in the territory where these operations were conducted or, rather, where there was a conflict, a war, a civil war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Please stop me if I am overstating the case, but does it come to this: An effort was made if Mr. Tadic's defence might have involved other people as yet undetected being named and being put at risk of arrest and prosecution themselves --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes, it boils down to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: -- that their existence or their names would be concealed even at the expense of putting forward Mr. Tadic's own personal defence in its best possible light?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. An effort was made with regard to the persons who were much, much higher up in the hierarchy than Mr. Tadic, that they should not be detected because they could bring down with them the leadership of the so-called Republika Srpska or of Yugoslavia, according to the principle of command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: From what you understood and your information from the source you've mentioned high up in the security service, what, if any, consideration was given by Mr. Vujin to Mr. Tadic's own interests as an accused person before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, he showed consideration to the assignment and task that he was given, that is to say, that Mr. Tadic in his statements, both to the investigators and before the Tribunal, should not expand the list of people responsible for what had happened in the region of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the territory of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: From the information that you saw and heard from this source, was Mr. Vujin representing Mr. Tadic to the best of his ability, or was Mr. Vujin representing, if I can put it this way, the interests, good or bad, of his state?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: He was not representing the interests of the state but tried to represent the interests of the ruling powers, the regime, the representatives of that state. We know that they are all accused by this Tribunal, stand accused by this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: If the interests of the regime conflicted with his duty to his client, Mr. Tadic, from the information you received which would come first, the regime or his client, Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: The regime, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I must ask you this: You have referred to a source or sources of information high up in the security service. You were asked by Their Honours earlier on whether you could, if I can put it bluntly, name names. I'm conscious, of course, that this court is in public and in open session. May I be permitted to put it this way, and it would not be my decision, it would be a decision for Their Honours: If this court were to go into closed session and you were permitted to write a name or names on a piece of paper to be shown to Their Honours, would you consider, Mr. Brkic, would you consider putting on a piece of paper the name or names of your source, sources high up in the secret service?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: If that paper is accessible to Mr. Vujin, then I would be signing the death sentence for those people, the people whose names I can write down. If you think you can bear them on your conscience, then I will do so, I mean, the Tribunal. I hope that the Honourable Tribunal will bear in mind the fact of the country that I live in and that the key people within that state, within that country, occupying the top posts are accused of the worst crimes committed in the history of humankind, and you're asking me to do something that places me in a very, very difficult situation, to be responsible for the lives of people, for the life of a man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Are you pressing this point, Mr. Abell?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm going to pass the buck, if I may be rude, to Your Honours. If Your Honours wish to go into closed session. It's a matter for Your Honours. We've heard the evidence of this gentleman as to why he feels he cannot unless very special circumstances apply. It would mean certain parties but not all parties in these proceedings seeing those names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, the court would feel safer to be guided by the counsel who is examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm not going to press it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: One last topic, Mr. Brkic. You mentioned earlier, in answer to me, about people higher up who needed to be protected. Did your source high up in the secret service, in the regime, did he indicate any names of individuals, however high up in the chain of things, who needed to be protected in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I think they were people who were -- Momir Talic, Mr. Brdjanin, and some other individuals who have not been imprisoned yet and the first who already have. So I don't want to incriminate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm not going to press that aspect any further. Mr. Brkic, I don't have, thank you very much, any further questions for you. Thank you. Would you wait there, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour. Mr. Brkic, to assist you in framing your answers, the time period, the relevant time period that we're concerned with for these proceedings is September of 1997 to April 1998. When I'm speaking or asking you questions, I'm referring to what you may have known during that -- or become aware of events that occurred during that time period. You refer to, just to go back to the last section of questions asked by Mr. Abell, your Exhibit 10, which is your statement of 18 February, 1999, the fact that that Mr. Vujin controlled evidence. What evidence that you know of did he control and when was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, in talks with his client, Mr. Tadic, acquired knowledge of what kind of direct knowledge his client had that took place in the events for which Mr. Tadic stands accused. He asked that his Defence counsel go and ascertain who was in command in the area, in command of the units, the police, the army, who had command responsibility in the crisis staffs, who could have committed a crime, who could have committed ethnic cleansing or transfer of the population. So Mr. Tadic, as a direct participant and somebody from the area, knew by name the people who, during that period of his indictment, were in the area at that time, and he asked that his Defence counsel should check this out and said that he, of course, did not commit the crime that he committed. Mr. Vujin, with his associate from his office, Mara Pilipovic, he entrusted her as his investigator and she would go to the area to talk to the people named by Mr. Tadic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: All of these specific areas which Mr. Tadic advised Mr. Vujin to investigate, you learned all of these specific questions from your source in the SDB?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes. He did not, of course, say whether everything that Mr. Tadic said was correct, that is to say, in the sense that he wasn't at such a place at such a time, but what was the defence, the overall defence of Mr. Tadic and which could have compromised others and possibly bring -- throw doubt, cast doubt on the participation of Mr. Tadic. That evidence did not turn up before the Tribunal or before Mr. Tadic, as the accused, as evidence in his favour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did your source from the SDB tell you how he became aware of these very particular instructions that Mr. Tadic had given to Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, as a lawyer who did not recognise the competencies of the International Tribunal, had strong contacts with the state police, with the secret police, and so in his work and presence at this Tribunal he, of course, wrote reports about that, and his contacts with the accused, the judges, the lawyers and so on. Everything was recorded in detail so that our police, that is to say, the police in Serbia, had insight into what was going on at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You also say that, in your statement, Mr. Vujin manipulated the evidence. What specific instances are you aware of that he manipulated particular evidence and when would that have occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: The man from the State Security Service that I talked to gave the assessment that on the basis of what he had before him, Mr. Vujin had been given a task and that he was fulfilling it very well, and that the evidence which would incriminate other people and which would throw doubt on the indictment of Mr. Tadic generally, then Mr. Vujin did away with that evidence. I was not personally interested in Mr. Tadic's case and people indicted for crimes, war crimes. I would just like the Tribunal to pass sentence as soon as possible, and I can't believe that they're so slow in doing so for people that are accused of murdering hundreds of people. So I personally wasn't interested to ask why, what witness and so on, because I would show a lack of trust towards the individual that was giving me this information. So I just heard his assessments and the information that he gave, and I took them to be absolutely correct but I did not enter into detail. As I say, I wasn't personally interested in Mr. Tadic's case in particular. He was accused of war crimes, and I was sure that the Tribunal would reach a judgement in the case. What I want to say, I did not take the testimonies of one witness or another witness. I didn't go into details, into any complete details because, as I say, it was an individual who wielded considerable influence and perhaps even decide on whether Mr. Vujin was to go ahead with his job or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So I take it then that your source in the SDB did not explain to you what the contents of any of these statements were that Mr. Vujin and his associates took, so you have no idea whether, in fact, they would have helped Mr. Tadic or hurt Mr. Tadic and his defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, at all events, it wouldn't have made it more difficult for him to defend himself because following some logics, Mr. Tadic would not have proposed somebody to be heard and to testify who would testify against him. So as I say, had I insisted, I could have obtained details, but as I personally was not interested in the case, then I was not interested in the details. I didn't want to burden myself with such names as Mita Mitrovic, just to quote an ad hoc example. I believed the man who was providing me with this information, because I considered him to be in the very peaks of the security service and that he was in charge of this operation, working with the lawyers, and that the information that he was giving me was, in fact, absolutely truthful. So in simplified terms, he told me that Mr. Vujin -- the evidence that Mara Filipovic had collected, his investigator, which indicated that other people had committed crimes in the area during the time of the indictment and for which Mr. Tadic was accused, that the reports and statements of those witnesses were given neither to Mr. Tadic nor to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
