utterances.text: Did you ever take it upon yourself to review the evidence actually submitted by Mr. Vujin in the Tadic case to determine if, in fact, he had submitted information which implicated others?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I do not know how Mr. Vujin -- in which way he defended Mr. Tadic and what evidence he submitted to the Tribunal, but I know that the security service has control over Mr. Vujin, and I was informed by the man there that Mr. Vujin had been given instructions to do away with that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keegan. Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, I'm going to pose my questions in Serbian, because I think that that will facilitate matters both because of the witness and for purposes of the interpretation as well, because they had some problems when I was speaking French earlier on today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell me please, Mr. Brkic, in what way you came to be a witness in this case, through your own initiative or through somebody else's initiative?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I was invited one day by a lawyer. I think I saw his name here somewhere. Vladimir Bosovic, that was the man. He called me and asked me -- he told me that he had read my text from the Srpska Rec, and he asked me how far it had gone with regard to the charge. I told him that -- of the court where the proceedings were going. I photocopied the charge brought by Mr. Toma Fila, and the judgement of the court, and the district court abolishing the charge, and the instructions given to the court of the first instance in its decision-making, and in that talk he told me that he was -- had been engaged by the defence counsel of Mr. Tadic to study the allegations made in the text with regard to the previous activities of Mr. Vujin, his professional activities, and he asked me to -- whether I would be ready to answer some of his questions. I answered -- he sent me his questions in writing, and I responded to those questions in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was it a case of the evidence that we had here today, Exhibits 9 and 10?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, Mr. Brkic, how long you have been a journalist? When did you start working as a journalist? I suppose you're a journalist today.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I started working in 1978. I got a job as a journalist for the first time in 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us what schooling you've had?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I have graduated from the faculty of mathematics, but I don't know if the State Security Service gave you other information about me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Today you testified that there were 570 charges brought against you in courts in Yugoslavia, against you.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that also refer to charges brought against you and the papers you work for?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: No, only against myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So exclusively against you yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Both in civil actions and in criminal actions?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Of those actions, how many have been completed up till today?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that five are still ongoing, that judgments are pending in five cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that in only one case you were proclaimed guilty, that is to say, you had to pay a fine, if I recall correctly. What about all the other cases? Were you also -- were you found not guilty? Were the charges rejected, dismissed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, they were either dismissed -- in five cases the proceedings were interrupted because they were outdated and abolished by the higher courts, and in the meantime, the passage of time, that is to say, four years had gone by, and they were discontinued as outdated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So at this point in time, there are only five cases that are ongoing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you regularly go to court when you were called up, for the most part?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. On a regular basis I went when I was called. It's rather a large number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, that is why I have asked you the question, because it would appear that you appear in court every week.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not turn up for a court hearing on one occasion and I was fined by a judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, you told us that the individual that gave you the information in the State Security Service, that you saw a list of Yugoslav lawyers, Serbian lawyers compiled by the bar association as defence counsel for The Hague. Do you recall how many lawyers were on that list?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, that event took place five years ago, a little over four years, in actual fact, and I think I stipulate them all in the text, that is to say, the more important names, the ones that I thought would play the major role. I stipulated them in the text and they, in fact, did appear as defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, how many lawyers were on the list all in all if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I think about 13 or 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you now recall the lawyers that were concerned?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I stipulate this in my text.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about the other lawyers on the list?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, they're probably waiting. There will be other accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No. What I mean is did that same source tell that you these people were working for the security service as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, as to their daily activities, I wasn't really interested in them because there are other affairs that I deal with. I can't ask them all the time what their informers are doing. I'm not a clerk for relationships between the source and the informers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As far as I was able to understand, you received all this information from one individual in the State Security Service echelons?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When we're talking about Mr. Vujin, you said today that you saw him personally and talked to him personally and that your relations were good.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that our relations were correct. That is to say, we have no conflicting interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your letter which is Exhibit 10, under item 1, towards the end of item 1, we have your statement that you don't know Mr. Vujin personally and that you were not in contact and not in conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I met him once in Mr. Guberina's office. He was there with Mara Pilipovic. We were introduced there but we didn't discuss anything that could compromise our relations on the occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you wrote that you did not know him personally and that you had no contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I assessed that relationship as -- by virtue of the fact that we did not have any business relations and he just happened to be in Mr. Guberina's office on the occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When did that meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I think it was four years previous to the event. That is to say, it would be sometime in 1990, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So in the same section you state that Mr. Vujin did not rebut any of the texts in which he was mentioned by you. However, today you said precisely that Mr. Vujin is one of the accusers in the 1995 charge brought against you for the article.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is accusing, but the paper would have denied this and the paper would have said that the quotations were not correct. Well, he did not accuse me, he accused the paper, and if somebody thinks he has been slandered, then the natural thing to do would be for the paper to publish a denial. That is the easiest way in which an injustice can be corrected, but as you can see, the proceedings are ongoing today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The paper Srpska Rec, did it publish a denial?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is regulated bylaw. If there is no denial, then the court can order it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. I know the legal provisions, but I'm asking you whether your newspaper published any denials.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not the editor in chief and have nothing to do with the editorial policies of my newspaper. So as denials and the way in which they are published are regulated by law, then the length of the denial must be directly proportionate to the article published. You are a lawyer and you know the rules and regulations governing that and the fines that a magistrate can enforce. All of that is regulated by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That's precisely why I'm asking you this question, Mr. Brkic, because Srpska Rec refused to publish a denial and that is why charges were brought against it. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I am not the editor in chief of the Srpska Rec newspaper, and whether the editor refused to publish a denial -- the newspaper carries 50 texts every time, which means that there are many individuals quoted for different things in the articles published. Now, whether the Srpska Rec newspaper published any denials or not, as far as I know, it did publish readers' letters, the letters of readers, and these reactions by the public were published if their contents were in order. You would have to ask the editor in chief of Srpska Rec because I, as a journalist, cannot decide on what is to be published in the newspaper and what is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you recall being a witness in a case of this kind, that is to say, when charges were brought against the Srpska Rec, when denials were not published and it was a case of one of your articles? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember which case it was?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: It was the case of Mrs. Borka Vucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know how the case ended?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: No, I do not. I know that the proceedings were ongoing and that Mrs. Vucic, who was an individual whom -- the international community forbade her to leave the country because she is the personal banker of Mr. Milosevic, and she is responsible for many millions that were looted, and she is one of the basic criminals that jeopardised the vital interests of the people and country that I live in. She brought charges against me, that is to say, she brought charges against the newspaper Srpska Rec, and these proceedings are being tended by the Ana Popovic chamber in the court in Belgrade and have not been concluded, and I say this with full responsibility. You can check this out, you can check out the case that exists, but a judgement has not been made yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I suggest that you ask your last question for this afternoon? One of our colleagues has another judicial appointment, and so we have to conclude at about now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My last question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting you should terminate your examination, but just for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I understand very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. Brkic: Unfortunately, what you have just said is not true.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I leave it to the Court to assess.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The Court shall assess it, and that particular case, those particular proceedings that you mentioned with Mrs. Borka Vucic, have been ended, and a judgement was made by the district court in Belgrade and the Supreme Court of Serbia, and Srpska Rec, because of your alleged interviews with Mrs. Vucic, was found guilty. It states that you thought up three interviews with Mrs. Vucic, and it was proven that you never saw Mrs. Vucic, nor could you have ever talked to her, and you published three interviews which had been judged invented by you, and I am going to hand over to the Tribunal this as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: May I answer those allegations?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You can see this, this evidence, this proof, if you so desire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do you want to answer?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, the judgement that Mr. Vujin's counsel is giving you was brought for corrections, and in that case, it is not up to the court to determine the truthfulness of the allegations but whether there were valid circumstances for the text to be published, that is to say, whether the text was signed by an individual to whom the information refers, whether the text is equal in length or proportionate in length, and you will be able to see that the court orders Srpska Rec to publish denials. It does not enter into the fact of whether it was true or not. This is done in criminal proceedings, that is to say, whether the allegations and quotations were correct or not, and this is a criminal proceeding, but in the civil proceedings, in the civil reports, this is a different matter, and that they cause psychological damage to the individual concerned. I'm sure that in reading the documents, you will be able to see that the court is merely ascertaining whether conditions have been met for a denial to be published and whether this particular lady has the right to a published denial. We live in a country in which key individuals have been accused of war crimes, amongst them judges, and most judges have been denied the right to leave the country. As I live in a country where there are no independent courts of law, then how could I have won these cases? So I should like to ask you to read the documents carefully, and what counsel has just stated is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Have you seen the document, Mr. Brkic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is not a question of criminal liability. They are separate proceedings which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you whether you have seen the document.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, are you marking them?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I have marked them, Your Honour. The first document of the 29th of April, 1998 will be Exhibit 12, and the second document under the heading "Gz. 82/97" will be Exhibit 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Any objections to admission? Then the documents are admitted. The Court will now rise until 10.00 tomorrow when we shall resume. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
